overview.summary: Recursion is a method where the solution to a problem depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem.
learningObjectives: Understand the absolute necessity of a Base Case.
Trace the Call Stack during recursive execution.
Convert iterative loops into recursive calls.
Understand the Choose -> Explore -> Unchoose pattern.
overview.interviewRelevance: Recursion is the engine behind Depth-First Search (DFS), Backtracking, and Dynamic Programming. You cannot pass a top-tier interview without mastering it.

paragraphs: Imagine you are in a line of people and want to know your position. You ask the person in front of you 'What is your position?'. They don't know either, so they ask the person in front of them.
Eventually, the person at the very front says 'I am number 1!'. Then the person behind them says 'I am 1 + 1 = 2!'. The answers bubble all the way back to you.
realWorldHook.ahaMoment: A recursive function pauses its own execution, asks a clone of itself for the answer to a smaller problem, and waits for the clone to finish.

definition.technicalDefinition: In computer science, recursion is a programming technique using function or algorithm that calls itself one or more times until a specified condition is met at which time the rest of each repetition is processed from the last one called to the first.

vocabulary.definition: The condition that stops the recursion. Without it, you get an infinite loop.
The part of the function where it calls itself with modified arguments.
The hidden memory structure the computer uses to keep track of paused recursive functions.

keyProperties: Uses implicit space O(Depth) on the Call Stack.
Often elegant but can be slower than iteration due to function call overhead.
Vulnerable to Stack Overflow if the base case is faulty or the depth is too large.

metaphor: Russian Nesting Dolls. You keep opening dolls until you find the solid one in the middle (Base Case). Then you assemble them back together.
mentalModel.clickSentence: Never try to trace the entire recursion tree in your head. Trust that the recursive call will return the correct answer for the subproblem, and just handle the current step.

memoryDescription: Every time a function calls itself, the computer pushes a new 'Frame' onto the Call Stack.
This frame contains all the local variables for that specific execution.

steps.explanation: Interactive Call Stack visualization coming soon.

operations.name: The Descent (Pushing to Stack)
operations.description: The function calls itself, creating a deeper, smaller problem.
operations.visualNote: A new frame appears on top of the stack.

operations.name: The Ascent (Popping from Stack)
operations.description: The base case is hit, and functions start returning values to the functions that called them.
operations.visualNote: Frames resolve and disappear, passing data downward.

operations.name: Choose
operations.description: Make a decision. Add the choice to your current state tracking.
operations.visualNote: A node is added to the active path.

operations.name: Explore
operations.description: Recurse deeper into the tree with the new state.

operations.name: Unchoose
operations.description: Undo the decision. Remove the choice from the state so the loop can try the NEXT choice.
operations.visualNote: The node is removed, and the pointer steps back.

patternTemplate.whenToUse: Whenever a problem can be broken down into identical, smaller subproblems. (Trees, Graphs, Divide & Conquer).

recognitionQuiz.problemStatement: You need to traverse a Tree data structure to find its maximum depth.
recognitionQuiz.explanation: Trees are inherently recursive data structures (a tree is made of smaller trees). Recursion is the most natural way to traverse them.

examples.title: Reverse Linked List (Recursive)
examples.problemStatement: Reverse a singly linked list using recursion.
steps: Base Case: If head is null or head.next is null, return head.
Recursive Step: Trust that calling `reverse(head.next)` will reverse the rest of the list and return the new head.
Cut the old forward pointer: `head.next = null`.

code.python:
def reverseList(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverseList(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

examples.rationale: This forces you to truly understand the Call Stack. The 'newHead' (the original tail) bubbles up untouched, while the actual pointer reversal happens during the ascent.

examples.title: Subsets
examples.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set).
steps: Create a backtrack function that takes a start index and current path.
Add a COPY of the current path to the result.
Loop from start index to end of nums.
Add num to path, recurse with index + 1, then pop num from path.
examples.rationale: There are 2^N subsets. For each element, we have a binary choice: include it or don't include it.

conceptQuiz.question: What is a Stack Overflow?
options: When an array gets too large.
When a recursive function calls itself too many times without hitting a base case, exhausting the computer's memory.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Every recursive call allocates a tiny bit of memory for its local variables. If you forget a base case, it loops forever until memory runs out and the OS kills the program.

conceptQuiz.question: Why is Recursion sometimes considered 'worse' than Iteration (Loops)?
options: Recursion cannot solve as many problems as loops.
Recursion uses implicit O(Depth) memory for the Call Stack, while a standard loop uses O(1) memory.
conceptQuiz.explanation: While recursion is elegant, it has an overhead cost. Anything that can be done recursively CAN be done iteratively (often by using your own explicit Stack data structure).

conceptQuiz.question: Why MUST we copy the array (e.g., `path[:]` or `[...path]`) before adding it to the final results?
options: Because it makes the code run faster.
Because arrays are passed by reference. If we don't copy it, the final result will just be a list of references to the exact same empty array after all the `.pop()` calls.
To satisfy the compiler's type checker.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If you just do `res.append(path)`, every entry in `res` points to the same object in memory. Since Backtracking pops everything off at the end, your answer will just be `[[], [], []]`.

conceptQuiz.question: What is 'Pruning' in a Backtracking algorithm?
options: Removing duplicates from the final answer.
Returning early from a branch if you know it cannot possibly be valid, saving time.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If you are trying to find combinations that sum to 10, and your current path sums to 15, there is no point exploring deeper. You 'prune' the branch by returning immediately.

practice.title: Fibonacci Number
practice.keyInsight: The textbook definition of recursion: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2).

practice.title: Pow(x, n)
practice.keyInsight: Fast exponentiation. If n is even, x^n = (x^2)^(n/2).

practice.title: K-th Symbol in Grammar
practice.keyInsight: The parent of a node at index K is at index K/2.

practice.title: Permutations
practice.keyInsight: Loop over ALL elements, but skip ones already in the path.

practice.title: Combination Sum
practice.keyInsight: You can reuse elements, so pass `i` down the recursion instead of `i+1`.

practice.title: N-Queens
practice.keyInsight: Classic backtracking. Place a queen, check validity, recurse, remove queen.
